dod_intent_evidence: Own SBIR Phase II abstract: '2022 Air Force ($749,999) — MicroLED-based Wearable Displays to Support Rapid Sustainment' names Department of the Air Force aircraft maintenance groups as the explicit customer for maintainer heads-up displays.
score_evidence: '40k full-color pixels per mm2 ... 5 nano-second response time ... 10x more brightness' → lab_language_intensity (dense spec-sheet bravado, zero operational framing)

blind_spots.blind_spot: No ATO/RMF/STIG/CMMC language despite the device being designed to stream Tech Order data wirelessly and enable real-time collaboration on what would have to be government networks.
blind_spots.operator_reality: Connecting to flightline systems and streaming technical data over wireless links onto DoD networks requires an ATO before any maintenance unit can actually use it — without that groundwork the 'future real-time collaboration with local and remote experts' promise stalls indefinitely regardless of how good the optics are.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Ostendo is fundamentally a photonics/chip company (QPI microLED IP since 2005) messaging toward consumer/enterprise AR first; the SBIR is a bolt-on defense application of the same core tech.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: connect wirelessly to existing laptops and tablets to stream existing Tech Order data to the glasses... this solution will enable real-time collaboration with local and remote experts

blind_spots.blind_spot: Zero SWaP-C or ruggedization specificity for a flightline maintenance environment — no mention of drop survivability, dust/grease/glove compatibility, or battery life through a shift.
blind_spots.operator_reality: A maintainer with grease-covered gloves on a flightline in variable weather needs a device built for that environment; the published spec sheet (brightness, FOV, pixel density) is consumer/enterprise-framed and never addresses ruggedization or field battery logistics.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: Ostendo explicitly positions as a horizontal core-technology supplier, not a device integrator: 'Ostendo is a core technology company and will not be selling Ostendo-branded glasses' — someone else is left to solve the ruggedization problem, and no partner/integrator is named.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: Ostendo is a core technology company and will not be selling Ostendo-branded glasses.

blind_spots.blind_spot: No mention of who trains the maintainer, how the device is sustained/repaired in the field, or GFE integration beyond a generic 'wirelessly connects to existing laptops and tablets' claim.
blind_spots.operator_reality: Fielding a new heads-up device into an Air Force aircraft maintenance group requires training curricula, spares logistics, and real integration with existing GFE toolchains — none of which appears anywhere in the pack despite the SBIR explicitly targeting that exact operator population.
blind_spots.why_likely_missing: The abstract is written to win the SBIR (technical novelty, patent portfolio) rather than to plan the fielding path.
blind_spots.evidence_quote: The Department of the Air Force, and specifically aircraft maintenance groups, have a national Defense-related need to accelerate problem resolution and improve training.

opener_hook: Ostendo's 2022 Air Force Phase II SBIR ($749,999) proposes streaming Tech Order data to maintainer-worn glasses via existing laptops and tablets — the abstract never says how that data gets an ATO to move on a government network.
what_they_do: Designs QPI microLED microdisplay chips and wearable-display reference designs for consumer/enterprise/defense AR glasses; the SBIR line builds maintainer heads-up displays for Air Force aircraft maintenance.
